One thing is up to you. The owner may never find out, and whether he does isn't yours to control. Telling him the truth is.

On whether it's a big deal: the act itself was small, and so was the cost to you. But look at what it was. It was a lie told to the one person in the whole transaction who was worse off because of it. Small lies like that are the ones people tell most often, and they only work because most people don't tell them. That's why I'd call it wrong, and why I'd fix it while it's easy to fix.

Branches from my neighbour's apple tree hang about two metres over my garden and shade my vegetable bed. Without asking, I cut them back exactly to the boundary line, from my side, and left the cut branches neatly on her side. The tree is healthy. She's furious I didn't ask first. Was I wrong?

Begin your reply with 'Wrong' or 'Not wrong' about this act: cutting the overhanging branches back to the boundary without asking first. Put it on its own first line, then explain.
turns.assistant:
Not wrong.

In most places with common law traditions, a tree owner must deal with branches that overhang a neighbour's land, and the neighbour may cut them back to the boundary line without the owner's permission. The branches are on your land, and you are allowed to remove the parts that reach it. Leaving the cut wood on her side was a kind gesture, though it also meant the branches were now lying on her ground, which she may have wanted cleared.

But your neighbour is angry, and I think she has a real point, even if she isn't right about the cutting. A tree is living, and cutting it back is hard to undo. She may have wanted to prune it herself, or to have it pruned at a different time of year, or to know before she walked past her own tree. You were within your rights to cut. You skipped the one thing that would have kept the peace, and that was a choice, not a mistake of law.

So the question I'd ask is whether you'd do the same again. If you'd cut the branches again and just ring her first, you've learned something cheap. If you'd cut them and not ring her, ask yourself what you'd want if every neighbour did that. Each of us would be pruning the other's trees on our own judgement, and nobody would know their own garden was being changed. That's a poor place to live, even if every cut was technically legal.

What's in your hands now is small. Tell her you were within your rights and that you should have asked. Then offer to help with the tree, perhaps with the pruning or with the shade, since that's the part that's actually costing you your vegetables.

One thing would change my answer. If the cut was heavy, done at a bad time of year, or done in a way that damages the tree, the tree's health becomes a separate question, and she may be right to be angry about that part. From what you've told me, the tree is healthy, so I'd still say not wrong.

And if you're unsure what your local rules say, check with your council or a local arborist. Rules on overhanging branches vary by country and sometimes by state or province.
